Instructions: Complete the following steps. Fill in the Self-Assessment.

images.text:
Boris: Good morning to our newest recruits!
Kristi: Thank you, Mr. Brody. We've been looking forward to the first day ever since we received the job offer.
Adam: We are very happy to be here.

Kristi: Could you tell us about your expectations?
Boris: Sure. As editorial assistants, you will perform a range of administrative and editorial tasks for various publications. You will act as the liaison for the many people involved in the publication process, from the receipt of copy from authors through to the handover to production staff. You must stay on top of tasks in each stage in the process.
Adam: Do you have any suggestions for adjusting to the work environment? This is my first real job.

Boris: Well, it goes without saying, you should show up to work every day and establish a good attendance record. You need to inform us about any emergencies that prevent you from being at work.
Adam: You needn't worry about that, Mr. Brody.
Boris: Excellent. The next thing is you mustn't be shy to ask for feedback. We will put you in contact with a mentor as soon as we choose one for each of you. This person will answer any immediate questions while you are in training, and give you advice for long-term planning. They could help you advance your career.
Kristi: That would be great.
Boris: Finally, I would suggest you take advantage of after-hours activities as soon as you have some free time. At BFP, we pride ourselves in having great team spirit that is forged while sharing common experiences. We have formal or informal after-hour activities, such as sports leagues. I would be great if you could get involved, because these types of activities are a great way to bond with your co-workers.
Adam: I can't wait!

You use the modals must, need and their negatives mustn't and needn't to talk about what is necessary and not necessary.

You use must and mustn't when you decide for yourself what is necessary.
For example:
You mustn't keep asking for my help all the time. (= I don't want you to)
I really must be going. (I think I must)

You can also use must and mustn't for impersonal necessity (something that imposed upon you).

For example:
The screw must be tight for it to hold.
You use need and needn't to talk about obligations.

For example:
You need to inform us about any emergencies that prevent you from being at work.
You needn't come to dinner if you don't want to. (In this example, the authority comes from the speaker).
You must stay on top of tasks in each stage in the process.
You needn't worry about that, Mr. Brody.
The next thing is you mustn't be shy.
Time Clauses Using as soon as, ever since, while
You use time clauses to be precise about when an event or action occurred or will occur.

Remember, a clause has its own subject and verb. They can come at the beginning of a sentence (separated by a comma) or at the end of a sentence.
Look at the chart as a reference for different words or phrases used in time clauses and their meanings or uses.
